Triggers.value: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure

go over and over why the event happened to me

issues.item: Triggers: Male Presence: Being alone with men
issues.explanation: 'Being alone with men' is difficult to reconcile with the indexed trauma of a child's life-threatening illness. It suggests an interpersonal or sexual threat context not reflected anywhere else in the profile, making it clinically hard to explain as a trauma-linked trigger for this patient.

issues.item: Threat: Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places
issues.explanation: 'I only feel safe in a very limited number of places' implies broad environmental danger and fits better with assault/attack-related trauma than a child's medical crisis. In this profile it does not connect plausibly to the other trauma-linked items and overstates place-based threat without supporting triggers or memories.

issues.item: Memory: Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event
issues.explanation: Auditory re-experiencing of sounds from the event is not impossible in medical trauma, but here it sits awkwardly alongside the selected triggers and threat items, which mainly imply interpersonal/male-danger and restricted-safe-place themes. This makes the memory content poorly matched to the rest of the profile and trauma context.

issues.item: Triggers: Feeling Happy: Feeling happy or relaxed
issues.explanation: 'Feeling happy or relaxed' as a trigger is hard to reconcile with the specified trauma type of a child's life-threatening illness and with the other selected triggers (loss of control, pregnancy/birth reminders). For this trauma, reminders tied to the child, illness, hospitals, uncertainty, or vulnerability are plausible; happiness/relaxation as a salient trigger is possible but here feels clinically disconnected from the rest of the profile and the formulation.

issues.item: Memory: Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
issues.explanation: Intense guilt on recall is not well supported by the rest of the profile. There are no Negative Appraisal items endorsing self-blame, responsibility, or moral failure, and the trauma type (child's life-threatening illness) does not inherently imply guilt. Given Memory has minimal linkage in the formulation and the rest of the profile centers on danger/loss of control rather than culpability, this guilt item appears insufficiently integrated with the overall self-report.

issues.item: Memory: Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, these two items describe opposing emotional states during recall—detached/numb recall versus intensely overwhelmed recall. Although fluctuation can occur, selecting both as core memory features without any qualifier is internally inconsistent enough to question whether they characterize the same patient's trauma memory profile.

issues.item: Triggers: Pregnancy/Birth Reminders: Pregnancy, childbirth, or babies in general
issues.explanation: Pregnancy/birth/babies reminders are hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of a child's life-threatening illness in a 75-year-old woman unless the medical crisis specifically centered on pregnancy or birth, which is not indicated. The other trigger items point to loss of control and uncertainty around illness, making this trigger stand out as trauma-incongruent.

issues.item: Memory: Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
issues.explanation: The memory set is not fully coherent with the trauma type. A child's life-threatening illness is usually an extended, medically focused stressor rather than a single visually dominated event; endorsing predominantly image-based, nonverbal trauma memory is less plausible unless there was a discrete acute medical crisis. Combined with the childbirth-related trigger, this begins to suggest a different trauma context.

issues.item: Memory: Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
issues.explanation: The two rumination items are difficult to reconcile with the formulation because Negative Appraisals is not active and has no outgoing/incoming edges, yet these strategies rely heavily on appraisal-based meaning-making and counterfactual blame. In this profile, maladaptive strategies are meant to feed threat directly; avoidance of emotional stress fits that pattern, but prevention/meaning rumination suggests an active appraisal system that is otherwise absent.

issues.item: Prevention Rumination: I dwell on how the event could have been prevented
issues.explanation: The two rumination items imply a strong negative-appraisal/meaning-making focus (preventability, why it happened to me), but Negative Appraisals is entirely unrepresented and specified as inactive in the formulation. That level of appraisal-focused processing is hard to reconcile with a profile where the active pattern is mainly Triggers → Threat and Negative Appraisals has no active role.

issues.item: Rumination: Meaning: go over and over why the event happened to me
issues.explanation: For a trauma involving a child's life-threatening illness, 'Cannot Trust Safety' is possible, but in this profile the triggers are specific medical uncertainty/procedures and the memory items are about overwhelm and replay; the item suggests a broad, generalized inability to believe safety assurances that is stronger and less context-linked than the rest of the profile. Given the formulation's strong Triggers → Threat link, a more trigger-bound threat style would be expected than this global safety-belief item.
